## pqac-00000037

From text 'genau2004microstructuraldevelopmentin pages 18-22'.

Amber Lynn Genau. Microstructural development in al-si powder during rapid solidification. ArXiv, Dec 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/835374, doi:10.2172/835374. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt identifies the HPGA gas atomization system as having three principal sections: a melt chamber, a spray chamber, and a powder collection system. The melt chamber uses a high-purity alumina crucible and stopper rod, with a zirconia-coated pour tube guiding the molten Al-Si alloy through a 1.7 mm orifice to the HPGA nozzle. The nozzle has an annular arrangement of 30 gas jets around the melt feed tube. At the nozzle, the high-velocity gas creates a wake and local low-pressure region, while recirculating flow acts opposite to the melt-stream direction. These effects cause the stream to spread into a thin film, split, and accelerate outward, promoting atomization. However, this excerpt does not provide the detailed HPGA layout requested for a collection canister or cyclone separator, nor does it describe how collected powder is specifically protected from liquid-metal splatter or un-atomized melt. It only establishes that a separate powder collection system follows the spray chamber and that melt disintegration occurs near the nozzle and atomization zone.

Huimin Wang1,2    & Boian T. Alexandrov2 & Eric Przybylowicz2,3


Received: 17 December 2018 /Accepted: 22 February 2019 /Published online: 4 March 2019
# International Institute of Welding 2019

Abstract
Finite element analysis (FEA) model of the solidification process in the cast pin tear test (CPTT) was developed using the
commercial software ProCAST™. Modeling predictions of the solidification and strain accumulation sequences and of the
cracking sensitive region location were validated using parallel CPTT testing of Alloy 52M filler metal. Predicted pin length
dependences of the hot tearing indicator (HTI) and the effective plastic strain (EPS) were in good correlation with the experi-
mentally determined zero to 100% CPTT cracking curve in Alloy 52 M. Sensitivity study with the developed model identified
material properties and test parameters with strong influence on the accuracy of modeling predictions. Parallel computational
modeling and CPTT experimentation was performed to quantify the critical strain for solidification cracking in Alloy 52M filler
metal. This study demonstrated that numerical modeling of weldability tests can be used for quantification of material-specific
properties related to cracking susceptibility in engineering alloys.

Journal of Achievements in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering, 116:11-24, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393, doi:10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393. This article has 41 citations.

The excerpt describes a closed ultrasonic atomization system relevant to powder production, although it does not specifically identify the AMAZEMET system, aluminium bronze, a cooling cone, or detailed splatter-protection and container geometry. The atomization chamber contains the sonotrode, electric-arc melting zone, and cooled inert-gas flow. Molten-metal droplets are ejected into the cooled inert gas, where surface tension forms nearly spherical particles; the droplets then cool, solidify rapidly, and are carried toward the chamber outlet by aerodynamic forces. The warm gas and powder stream is sent to a cyclone separator. Powder is collected beneath the cyclone in a sealed container, while the gas is filtered to remove fine dust, cooled, and recirculated. The equipment is described as having separate raw-material delivery, melting, ultrasonic, cooling-gas/atomization-chamber, and gas-powder separation subsystems. The chamber operates under an inert-gas atmosphere, including during electric-arc ignition. The source indicates that integrated melting and atomization on the sonotrode helps avoid splashing associated with melting material above the sonotrode and draining it downward; earlier arrangements could produce interrupted atomization and poor-quality powder. However, no specific design details for a cooling cone, splash guard, container sealing mechanism, or AMAZEMET aluminium-bronze configuration are provided in this excerpt.

The excerpt describes powder collection in the AMAZEMET rePowder ultrasonic atomization process in general, but it does not specifically discuss aluminium bronze. During atomization, molten droplets are ejected from the sonotrode and transported by a low-pressure argon stream. They solidify while airborne, before contacting any surface, which is presented as a means of producing high-purity spherical powder. The passage does not provide a detailed chamber layout, cooling-cone geometry, container design, or dedicated splatter-protection system. It does mention post-process handling: unatomized material is removed with a sieve having a 200 µm mesh opening. In arc-melting operation, metal vapor condenses on the chamber interior; this light, submicron deposit is removed by shaking, sonication, and rinsing before drying. These cleaning steps remove tiny high-surface-area particles and improve chemical properties. The excerpt therefore provides limited information relevant to collection and chamber cleanup, but no explicit engineering details about a cooling cone, collection container, or splash/splatter shielding.

Journal of Achievements in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering, 116:11-24, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393, doi:10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393. This article has 41 citations.

The excerpt provides only general information relevant to the AMAZEMET ultrasonic atomization process. Atomization occurs inside a cooled atomization chamber under an inert-gas atmosphere. The molten metal is delivered onto a cooled sonotrode, where ultrasonic vibrations destabilize capillary waves and eject molten droplets. The droplets initially pass through very hot gas, above 3000 K, and remain liquid briefly; surface tension rounds them into spherical particles before they cool and crystallize into powder. The passage does not describe the downstream powder-collection arrangement, the detailed chamber geometry, a cooling cone, the design of the receiving container, or any splatter-protection features. It also does not specify whether powder is collected in a removable vessel, cyclone, filter, or other separation system. Therefore, while it supports describing the atomization zone as an inert-gas, cooled-chamber environment with a cooled sonotrode and droplet cooling, additional AMAZEMET-specific documentation would be needed to answer the questions about powder collection, cooling-cone construction, container design, and protection against molten-metal splatter.

Andrei Yankin, Hussain Ali Murtaza, Boris Golman, Asma Perveen, and Didier Talamona. Effect of ultrasonic atomization parameters on alsi12 aluminum powder characteristics for additive manufacturing. Scientific Reports, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7. This article has 5 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes powder collection in an ultrasonic atomization system, although it concerns AlSi12 aluminum powder produced with an ATO Lab + US35 rather than AMAZEMET aluminum bronze. A wire is fed near an electric arc, which melts the material on a vibrating platform. Ultrasonic vibrations spread the molten metal into fine droplets, which solidify into powder. The droplets are dispersed through an atomization chamber and collected in a designated powder container. The excerpt does not provide detailed construction information for the chamber, such as its dimensions, internal geometry, atmosphere, or materials. It also does not mention a cooling cone, a specific container design, or dedicated splatter-protection features. The only related geometric control described is adjustment of the electric-arc position, which changes the angle at which molten droplets travel through the chamber into the collection container; this angle ranges from −5° to 5° relative to the electrode axis. After collection, the powder is sieved through a 63 μm mesh, with particles below that size considered suitable for the laboratory’s Renishaw AM400 SLM system. Approximately 75% of the produced powder became usable material.

function.name: create_artifact

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Thermal analysis table showing equilibrium temperatures for different container configurations receiving 816g C63000 bronze shot at ~1000°C. The calculation uses a first-law energy balance: Q_bronze = m_bronze × c_p_bronze × (T_initial - T_eq) = sum of [m_i × c_p_i × (T_eq - T_ambient)] for each container component.

Input assumptions to state:
- C63000 specific heat: ~420 J/(kg·K) (handbook value for Cu-Al-Ni bronze)
- 316L stainless steel specific heat: ~500 J/(kg·K)
- Copper specific heat: ~385 J/(kg·K)
- Bronze initial temperature: 1000°C (partly liquid shot)
- Ambient/container initial temperature: 25°C
- Latent heat of solidification for C63000 ~205 kJ/kg (estimate, Cu-alloy typical)
- All values marked as estimates

Rows/scenarios:
1. 816g bronze → 1 kg 316L container only: T_eq ≈ (0.816×420×1000 + 0.816×205000 + 1.0×500×25)/(0.816×420 + 1.0×500) ≈ include latent heat → ~510°C [EXCEEDS all elastomer limits]
2. 816g bronze → 1 kg 316L + 0.5 kg Cu puck: T_eq ≈ 380°C [EXCEEDS EPDM, near FKM limit]
3. 816g bronze → 1 kg 316L + 1.0 kg Cu puck: T_eq ≈ 310°C [EXCEEDS EPDM, FKM; within FFKM excursion]
4. 816g bronze → 3 kg 316L container: T_eq ≈ 280°C [within FFKM, exceeds FKM continuous]
5. 816g bronze → 3 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu puck: T_eq ≈ 220°C [within FKM excursion range]

Note: These are adiabatic equilibrium temperatures (worst case). Real temperatures will be lower due to radiation, conduction to cone, and argon convection. But the O-ring temperature depends on distance from the hot pile and thermal resistance of the liner/gap. Mark all as estimates with stated inputs."}

### Artifact (ID artifact-03)

```python
# Adiabatic, lumped-capacitance screening calculation.
# C63000 is reported to have solidus/liquidus temperatures of about
# 1043/1060 °C; therefore, applying latent heat to all material at an
# assumed 1000 °C is deliberately conservative. (pqac-00000039)

m_bronze = 0.816       # kg [estimate]
T_bronze = 1000.0      # °C [estimate]
T_ambient = 25.0       # °C [estimate]

cp_bronze = 420.0      # J/(kg·K), Cu-Al-Ni bronze estimate
latent_bronze = 205000 # J/kg, conservative Cu-alloy estimate
cp_ss316l = 500.0      # J/(kg·K), temperature-averaged estimate
cp_copper = 385.0      # J/(kg·K), temperature-averaged estimate

scenarios = {
    "1 kg 316L only":             {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 0.0},
    "1 kg 316L + 0.5 kg Cu":      {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 0.5},
    "1 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu":        {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 1.0},
    "3 kg 316L only":             {"ss316l": 3.0, "copper": 0.0},
    "3 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu":        {"ss316l": 3.0, "copper": 1.0},
}


def equilibrium_temperature(m_ss, m_cu, include_latent):
    """Return adiabatic equilibrium temperature in °C."""
    receiver_heat_capacity = m_ss * cp_ss316l + m_cu * cp_copper
    numerator = (
        m_bronze * cp_bronze * T_bronze
        + receiver_heat_capacity * T_ambient
    )
    if include_latent:
        numerator += m_bronze * latent_bronze

    denominator = m_bronze * cp_bronze + receiver_heat_capacity
    return numerator / denominator


print(f"{'Configuration':<30} {'Full latent heat':>18} {'No latent heat':>18}")
print("-" * 70)

for name, masses in scenarios.items():
    with_latent = equilibrium_temperature(
        masses["ss316l"], masses["copper"], include_latent=True
    )
    without_latent = equilibrium_temperature(
        masses["ss316l"], masses["copper"], include_latent=False
    )
    print(f"{name:<30} {with_latent:>15.1f} °C {without_latent:>15.1f} °C")

# Expected approximate output:
# 1 kg 316L only                    620.0 °C           421.0 °C
# 1 kg 316L + 0.5 kg Cu             508.8 °C           347.7 °C
# 1 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu               433.7 °C           287.1 °C
# 3 kg 316L only                    296.8 °C           206.1 °C
# 3 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu               249.5 °C           179.6 °C
#
# These are estimated bulk upper/lower bounds, not seal temperatures.
# Radiation, conduction into the water-cooled cone, and argon convection
# are omitted, while local metal-contact temperatures may initially be
# much higher than the calculated bulk equilibrium temperature.
```


*Code_block: Python calculates adiabatic equilibrium temperatures for five stainless-container and copper-puck configurations, both with a conservative full latent-heat allowance and without latent heat.*

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. A university lab runs an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room
pressure about 850-865 mbar). A 0.3-1.1 kg charge (aluminium alloys, and copper alloys such as
nickel-aluminium bronze UNS C63000 poured at about 1300 C) is induction-melted in a graphite crucible,
pushed through a 0.5 mm nozzle by argon over-pressure, and falls onto a plate vibrating at 40 kHz that
breaks it into powder (d50 roughly 100 um on good runs). Powder falls through a water-cooled stainless
cone under the chamber into a collection container that hangs from the cone's outlet flange on a
hinged clamp (ISO-KF style with a centring ring and O-ring, or possibly sanitary tri-clamp; size about
DN40-50, being confirmed). The chamber is evacuated to about 10 mbar absolute and backfilled with argon
several times, then runs at about +150 mbar gauge; a mechanical relief valve opens at +0.8 bar.
The stock container, top to bottom: the flange on a short neck, a conical reducer, a valve body with a
lever-operated flap valve whose seat is an EPDM ring, a borosilicate(?) glass tube about 100 mm across
in a perforated steel guard, sealed by elastomer rings in grooves of a top and a bottom stainless plate,
and four tie rods. A curved stainless splash plate sits in the bore at the top. The manufacturer also
supplies protective "shields" that fit in the cone; on the failed run they were not fitted and the
splash plate was in backwards.

The failure (Nov 13 2026): the plate barely atomized, so most of an 816 g C63000 charge left it as 1-3 mm
shot, still partly liquid when it reached the container about 0.4 s later. Bronze piled up at the
container's entrance; the glass glowed orange; the EPDM valve seat burned (white crust, smoke out of
the joint); the seals under the glass were damaged; the glass cracked at its top rim. Good runs never
damaged the container. The manufacturer says a "much simpler metal cup, without the glass" exists
(a stainless tube with a separate sanitary butterfly valve), and that in their own lab they mostly use
"the simple stainless steel" tube because it is easier to make and clean, but its delivery date is
unknown. The lab wants to build its own container within days to a few weeks, glass or metal.

The lab's design so far (to be reviewed, not assumed correct):
A. All-metal, catalogue parts only: a 316L ISO-KF full nipple (bore about 48 mm, 200-250 mm long) hung
   from the cone with the existing clamp; a KF blank flange at the bottom with a stainless centring ring
   and FKM O-ring; a drop-in 304/316 sacrificial liner sleeve in the top bore so that hot metal cannot
   touch the top O-ring; a loose copper or steel "catch puck" at the bottom to soak up heat and keep the
   pile off the bottom joint; Type K thermocouples clamped on the outside at the top flange and near the
   bottom, read by a panel meter with an alarm; no valve (a KF blank and clamp go on the top after
   removal), or a full-port valve whose seats are hidden behind the ball when open.
B. All-metal, turned and TIG-welded: one 316L vessel (KF weld stub, a 63-76 mm tube, a 10 mm welded
   bottom, no bottom seal), with an internal shoulder that locates the sacrificial liner.
C. Glass rebuild: the stock plates, valve and tie rods with a fused-quartz tube in place of the
   borosilicate, FKM or silicone seals, and a stainless liner sleeve that covers the glass rim and the
   top seal.

Review these designs and recommend one. Give numbers with sources (data sheets, standards, papers with
DOIs, vendor technical notes) and mark every estimate with its inputs.

1. Materials. 304 vs 316L for the body, liner and puck; copper or graphite as a liner or catch puck
   (wetting and sticking of molten copper alloys and aluminium on each; galling; contamination of the
   powder). Fused quartz vs borosilicate 3.3 for a 100 mm tube: thermal-shock limits, cost, and what
   happens if 1000 C metal touches it. Is a metal body clearly better for this duty?
2. Seals. Temperature limits (continuous and short excursions) of FKM, VMQ silicone, EPDM, FFKM and
   PTFE in KF centring rings and tri-clamp gaskets; which survive vacuum service to 10 mbar with low
   permeation; is a metal (aluminium or copper) KF seal or a spring-energised seal practical here? How
   far must an O-ring be from a hot pile, and how much does a metal centring ring between them help?
3. Heat. If 100-800 g of bronze shot at about 1000 C lands in the container, how hot do a 1 kg vs 3 kg
   stainless container, a copper puck, and the seals get, and how fast? What thermal mass, spacing or
   cooling (fins, water jacket, an argon purge) keeps the seals below their limits? Is a sacrificial
   liner worth it, and what gap and length should it have?
4. Valve. Does the container need an isolation valve at all for Al and Cu alloy powders that are
   emptied in air within an hour? If so, which type keeps its seals out of the falling metal (full-port
   ball valve with PTFE seats, butterfly, knife gate, flap)? What do gas-atomizer and powder-handling
   systems use for powder collection canisters (for example Ames Lab HPGA, commercial VIGA/EIGA units,
   AMAZEMET rePowder and similar), and how do they protect them from unatomized metal?
5. Sealing and leaks. ISO-KF vs sanitary tri-clamp for a joint that cycles between 10 mbar absolute
   and +150 mbar gauge: leak rates, clamp loads, how centring rings and gaskets behave after heating,
   and what a lab should check (rate-of-rise, soap at overpressure, helium) before trusting the O2
   reading.
6. Rank the risks of each design (A, B, C) for a lab that wants something working within days, and
   say what you would change.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll analyze this complex engineering question about designing a powder collection container for an ultrasonic atomizer. Let me create a comprehensive plan.

Abstract:
Graphite, a critical material for furnace walls, is pivotal to the reliability of the carbon-free hydrogen production industry through methane pyrolysis catalyzed by molten metals. This study systematically investigates the corrosion behavior of molten CuSn alloy on three typical commercial graphite materials—low-density graphite (LDG), high-density graphite (HDG), and pyrolytic graphite (PyG)—with a focus on their corrosion resistance and the underlying mechanisms responsible for graphite corrosion over a period of up to 1000 h at 1100 °C. The experimental results show that LDG suffered the most severe corrosion, with a mass loss of up to 60.09% and a hardness decrease from 0.73 GPa to 0.17 GPa, whereas PyG demonstrated the best corrosion resistance, with only a 5.64% mass loss and a hardness drop from 0.52 GPa to 0.35 GPa. SEM and XRD analyses revealed that the porous structures of LDG and HDG suffered significant macroscopic corrosion, caused by the stress from molten metal infiltration and aggregation in the pores, leading to structural collapse. Interestingly, all three types of graphite, including the non-porous PyG, exhibited disordered microstructural degradation as detected by Raman spectroscopy. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirmed that the thermal motion of Cu and Sn atoms primarily drives the microstructural corrosion of graphite, suggesting that the corrosion process involves both micro- and macro-level damage. These findings provide crucial insight into the compatibility of different graphite materials with molten CuSn alloy and valuable guidance for material selection in methane pyrolysis devices.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Glass, as an amorphous material with excellent optical transparency and chemical stability, plays an irreplaceable role in modern engineering and technology fields such as semiconductor manufacturing and micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS). For example, borosilicate glass, with a coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) that is close to having good thermal shock resistance and chemical stability, can be applied to MEMS packaging and aerospace fields. SiO2 glass exhibits excellent thermal stability, extremely low optical absorption, and high light transmittance, while also possessing strong chemical stability and extremely low dielectric loss. It is widely used in semiconductors, photolithography, and micro-optical devices. However, the stress sensitivity of traditional mechanical joints and the poor weather resistance of adhesive bonding make conventional methods unsuitable for glass joining. Welding technology, with its advantages of high joint strength, structural integrity, and scalability for mass production, has emerged as a key approach for precision glass joining. In the field of glass welding, technologies such as glass brazing, ultrasonic welding, anodic bonding, and laser welding are being widely studied and applied. With the advancement of laser technology, laser welding has emerged as a key solution to overcoming the bottlenecks of conventional processes. This paper, along with the application cases for these technologies, includes an in-depth study of common issues in glass welding, such as residual stress management and interface compatibility design, as well as prospects for the future development of glass welding technology.</jats:p>

Abstract:
High peak power laser systems are vulnerable to performance degradation due to particulate contamination on optical surfaces. In this work, we show using model contaminant particles that their optical properties decisively determine the nature of the optical damage. Borosilicate particles with low intrinsic optical absorption undergo ablation initiating in their sub-surface, leading to brittle fragmentation, distributed plasma formation, material dispersal and ultimately can lead to micro-fractures in the substrate optical surface. In contrast, energy coupling into metallic particles is highly localized near the particle-substrate interface leading to the formation of a confined plasma and subsequent etching of the substrate surface, accompanied by particle ejection driven by the recoil momentum of the ablation plume. While the tendency to create fractured surface pitting from borosilicate is stochastic, the smooth ablation pits created by metal particles is deterministic, with pit depths scaling linearly with laser fluence. A simple model is employed which predicts ~3x electric field intensity enhancement from surface-bound fragments. In addition, our results suggest that the amount of energy deposited in metal particles is at least twice that in transparent particles.

Abstract:
This paper aims to evaluate the thermal decomposition temperature and linear thermal expansion coefficient of typical non-metallic materials in aero-engine components. Thermogravimetric analysis and thermomechanical analysis were employed to systematically investigate the thermal and dimensional stability of these materials at varying heating rates, and their performance was validated through fireproof experiments. It was found that the high-strength graphite gasket exhibited the highest thermal decomposition temperature, while the polytetrafluoroethylene and fluorosilicone rubber showed excellent dimensional stability. Fluorine-based materials, such as fluorine rubber, showed higher thermal decomposition temperatures but relatively poor dimensional stability. This paper provides a scientific basis for the selection and design of sealing materials in aero-engines, contributing to the improvement of equipment safety and reliability.

The excerpt reports wetting behavior for molten copper and copper alloys on two carbon substrates—HX30 graphite and vitreous carbon—at approximately 1145 ± 5°C, within the requested temperature range. Pure molten copper remained non-wetting on both carbon surfaces; its contact angle decreased only slowly with time, possibly because of evaporation. Most 1 at.% copper alloys behaved similarly, with contact angles not differing by more than about 25° from pure copper. The exceptions were chromium additions on both HX30 graphite and vitreous carbon, and vanadium additions on vitreous carbon. These were the only alloy/substrate combinations producing rapid contact-angle changes and contact angles below 90°, indicating wetting. The study linked alloy reactivity to carbide formation: many alloying additions produced interfacial carbide reaction products, while the two effective wetting systems formed thin, continuous, coherent carbide layers. The excerpt does not provide measurements for stainless-steel surfaces, nor does it establish behavior across the full 1000–1300°C interval; therefore, no stainless-steel contact angles or reactivity conclusions can be extracted from this source.

Abstract:
The article presents the results of the development works and research on the atomization process carried out using two prototype high-power ultrasonic systems. Ultrasonic systems have been designed to develop a new metal powder production process; these materials are increasingly used in modern manufacturing processes such as additive technologies or spraying and surfacing processes. The preliminary studies presented in the article were conducted for water to assess the effectiveness of both systems and to verify the theoretical and structural assumptions. In ultrasonic atomization, the ultrasonic wave causes the phenomenon of cavitation, which leads to the overcoming of the surface tension forces of the liquid and its disintegration into fine droplets. The important parameters that affect the properties of the produced droplets include, among others, the frequency of the sonotrode vibrations and the amplitude of the vibrations of the working plate. As part of the research, the paper presents the process of selecting the sonotrode geometry for two different values of the transducer’s natural frequencies (20 kHz and 70 kHz). In the design process, the finite element method was used to perform a harmonic analysis and develop the geometry of the sonotrode and the working plate. The design assumptions and the design process were presented. The modeled and then ultrasonic waveguides were verified experimentally by measuring the deflection distribution on the working plate surface using a high-precision laser displacement sensor. Then, the work ultimately resulted in conducting atomization tests of water. The obtained aerosols and the mechanism of their formation were studied using a high-speed camera. Finally, using Matlab R2020a software and image analysis scripts, it was possible to analyze the droplet size distribution generated by both systems. It was observed that 50% of the produced droplets were in the range of 35–55 μm for a 20 kHz system, while for a 70 kHz system it was 10–25 μm, which is a very satisfying distribution in terms of metal powder atomization.

Abstract:
The adoption of additive manufacturing (AM) has driven extensive research into metal feedstocks, uncovering strong links between powder quality and the performance of printed parts. Poor powder characteristics, inadequate flowability or inconsistent packing, can significantly degrade the mechanical performance of the final 3D-printed components. This study investigates the effects of arc manipulator angle, electrical current, and vibration amplitude on AlSi12 powder quality via ultrasonic atomization (UA). Parameter adjustments significantly influenced particle size distribution, with span variations up to 37.5%. Optimal rheological properties were achieved by increasing the vibration amplitude (from 75 to 80%), decreasing the arc angle (from 5° to -5°), and reducing the current (from 150 A to 140 A). A modified AM suitability factor (AMS) was developed, incorporating logarithmic transformation and custom weighting to mitigate high-uncertainty parameter effects. Results revealed a non-linear relationship between powder suitability and arc angle, with a sharp worsening above 0°. Electrical current had the greatest impact on powder quality, followed by arc angle and vibration amplitude. Benchmarking showed that UA powder achieved suitability factors 21% higher than commercial powder, with improved sphericity compared to the irregular, fused particles of commercial alternatives. These findings underscore the potential of UA to enhance AM part reliability.

As the quality and the performance of AM manufactured functional products depend on the quality and the cost of the atomized metal or alloy powder used, the use of powders of high size uniformity, high purity, high sphericity, high flowability, low cost, and no trapped gas bubble porosity is necessary. Minor contamination and high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles, was observed in atomized powders. The innovative ultrasonic atomization method appears as a promising tool for material scientists to develop powders with tailored chemical composition, size and structure.

The excerpt provides detailed vacuum-service information mainly for FKM/Viton-A, while it does not provide comparative limits or outgassing data for FFKM, EPDM, silicone/VMQ, or PTFE. Viton is described as one of the most commonly used vacuum seals and as more durable than nitrile and other general-purpose elastomers. Its stated continuous service capability is 204°C, with short excursions to 315°C; dynamic sealing has been successful at –40°C, with some static capability down to –60°C. The excerpt gives a typical Viton-A outgassing rate of 152 (mbar·l·s⁻¹·cm⁻² ×10⁻⁸) after one hour in vacuum and 15 after five hours. Vacuum bakeout substantially lowers Viton O-ring outgassing: baking at 150–200°C for four hours can reduce rates from a few ×10⁻⁷ to a few ×10⁻¹⁰ torr·l·s⁻¹·cm⁻², with most evolved gas being water vapor. The text also notes that polymers and elastomers generally outgas far more than metals and glass, so their use should be minimized where practical. For comparison, mild baking at 100°C makes Viton approximately 50–60 times better than nitrile in the cited tests.

Abstract:
Metal powders are a fundamental starting point for fabricating many types of nuclear targets. Elemental powder properties can differ drastically between batches, even when using the same method. Therefore, the variation in morphology and the size of metal powders can cause variable quality and produce inconsistent results with what are otherwise proven target manufacturing techniques. Additive manufacturing has additional requirements for higher quality and more uniform feedstock. The production of spheroidized powders with uniform, reproducible properties and a narrow size distribution represents unexplored opportunities for experiments. These opportunities include experimenting with solid metals that can now flow like liquids, new options for powder handling and dispensing, and new target fabrication methods using additive manufacturing. The Stable Isotope Materials and Chemistry Group at Oak Ridge National Laboratory obtained an AMAZEMET rePowder ultrasonic metal atomization tool for creating limited batches of fully dense, free flowing, spherical powders with a narrow size distribution of extremely rare materials. Early results are presented with materials that were produced. The team explores the anticipated limits of this instrument with extremely rare materials (e.g., enriched stable isotopes) and highlights research into new fabrication techniques that provide additional options benefitting the international nuclear target community.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In the post-processing of large maritime components, a considerable amount of waste in the form of milling and grinding chips is produced. At the same time, additive manufacturing technologies have shown great potential in producing high-volume parts for maritime applications, allowing novel design approaches and short lead times. In this context, this study presents a sustainable approach to recycle and use aluminium bronze waste material, generated during post-processing of large cast ship propellers, as feedstock for laser-powder directed energy deposition. The recycling technology used to produce powder batches is inductive re-melting in combination with ultrasonic atomization. The derived metal powders are characterized using digital image analysis, powder flowability tests, scanning electron microscopy as well as energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Compared to conventional metal powders produced by gas atomization, the recycled material shows excellent sphericity and a powder size distribution with a higher content of finer and coarser particles. Metallographic sections of deposited additively produced specimens show an increased hardness and reduced ductility, but also competitive densities and higher yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to cast material. The process chain shows high potential for the maritime sector to enable circular and sustainable manufacturing.

Al-10Cu (wt%) rod and powder were prepared using the Amazemet rePowder system. A 90:10 by mass mix of pure aluminium and pure copper was used as feedstock for both rod and powder. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. The insights presented herein position UPA as a transformative solution for enabling sustainable, high-performance NiTi powder regeneration within AM workflows, advancing the circular economy in advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser Hot Wire (LHW) Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Additive Manufacturing (AM) processes are capable of manufacturing parts with a high deposition rate. There is a growing research interest in replacing large cast Nickel Aluminum Bronze (NAB) components using LHW DED processes for maritime applications. Understanding thermomechanical behavior during LHW DED of NAB is a critical step towards the production of high-quality NAB parts with desired performance and properties. In this paper, finite element simulations are first used to predict the thermomechanical time histories during LHW DED of NAB test coupons with an increasing geometric complexity, including single-layer and multilayer depositions. Simulation results are experimentally validated through in situ measurements of temperatures at multiple locations in the substrate as well as displacement at the free end of the substrate during and immediately following the deposition process. The results in this paper demonstrate that the finite element predictions have good agreement with the experimental measurements of both temperature and distortion history. The maximum prediction error for temperature is 5% for single-layer samples and 6% for multilayer samples, while the distortion prediction error is about 12% for single-layer samples and less than 4% for multilayer samples. In addition, this study shows the effectiveness of including a stress relaxation temperature at 500 °C during FE modeling to allow for better prediction of the low cross-layer accumulation of distortion in multilayer deposition of NAB.

Abstract:
There is increased interest in using nickel aluminum bronze (NAB) alloys in large-scale directed energy deposition additive manufacturing (DEDAM) processes for maritime applications, but one challenge lies in the component distortion that results from residual stress generated during fabrication. This paper describes the development and evaluation of thermo-mechanical simulations for laser hot wire (LHW) DEDAM of NAB to predict part distortion. To account for the dearth of temperature-dependent properties for NAB C95800 in open literature and public databases, temperature-dependent material and mechanical properties for NAB C95800 were experimentally measured using test specimens fabricated with a variety of DEDAM processes. Autodesk’s Netfabb Local Simulation software, a commercial finite-element based AM solver, was employed but with its heat source model modified to accommodate LHW DEDAM’s oscillating laser path and additional energy input supplied by the preheated wire feedstock. Thermo-mechanical simulations were conducted using both the acquired temperature-dependent material and mechanical properties and the constant room-temperature properties to assess the impact on simulation accuracy. The usage of constant properties in the thermo-mechanical analysis resulted in significantly different predicted distortion compared to those using the temperature-dependent properties, at times even predicting substrate displacement in an opposite direction.

The excerpt describes helium mass-spectrometer leak testing, which is directly relevant to evaluating vacuum-system and flange seal performance, including ISO-KF centring-ring seals. Helium is selected because it is small enough to penetrate very small cracks, chemically inert, non-toxic, inexpensive, and present in the atmosphere at only about 5 ppm, providing a low background. Helium leak detectors commonly measure leak rates from approximately 10^-4 to 10^-11 mbar·l/s, with the stated detection capability reaching 5×10^-12 mbar·l/s. In the analyzer cell, ions are separated according to mass in a magnetic field; the helium-ion current is proportional to helium partial pressure and is used to determine leak flow. For vacuum systems, the local helium-spray method is identified as the most suitable approach: the evacuated component is connected to the detector, while helium is sprayed locally around potential leak points. Helium entering through a defective seal produces a signal, and correlating the signal with spray-head position permits leak localization. The excerpt also notes that signal appearance is delayed and depends on the tested volume and helium throughput. It does not provide specific ISO-KF centring-ring seal acceptance limits or describe a rate-of-rise test, whose results would instead be based on pressure increase over time.

It distinguishes real leaks, caused by actual holes, cracks, poorly seated gaskets, or permeation, from virtual leaks caused by internal desorption, vaporization, moisture, or contamination. For a real leak, the pressure rise after isolation is expected to be approximately linear; its slope depends on the leak rate and system volume. A larger leak produces a steeper pressure-rise slope, while a larger volume produces a shallower slope. A virtual leak typically produces a pressure-rise curve that becomes shallower with time and may disappear after the system is re-pumped. The text recommends assembling the vacuum system and using mass-spectrometry helium leak detection to quantify very small leaks, since direct flow measurement is impractical. It also notes that even minor leaks can substantially limit the attainable pressure. Abstract:
Although aluminum bronze exhibits considerable wear and mechanical properties, nickel-aluminum bronze displays superior performance. A potential issue is the resistance to wear, particularly whether the addition of silicon (Si) enhances anti-wear properties. Samples with varying silicon content (0.2%, 0.4%, and 0.6%) were prepared in three conditions for the purpose of investigating the effects of silicon on wear and mechanical properties. The materials were forged and cast in accordance with the specifications set forth in JIS H 5120 for the production of specimens. The wear and mechanical properties were evaluated through a series of tests, including tensile strength, hardness, impact, and ball-on-disc wear tests. The results demonstrated that, in comparison to ASTM B148-52 or the precursor AlBC-3, as observed in nickel-aluminum bronze, the addition of silicon during the melting of the substrate resulted in a transformation of the precipitation of the kappa phase to α+κ. The intermetallic compounds were introduced to enhance the formation of pearlite. This resulted in an increase in the tensile strength and hardness of the metal, but a simultaneous decline in its ability to absorb impact. Furthermore, the wear test results indicated that the surface friction coefficient between the nickel-aluminum-bronze disc and the SUS304 stainless steel ball was associated with the amount of silicon added and the hardness. In other words, the workpiece friction coefficient would decrease with increasing hardness due to the rising silicon content. Additionally, it was observed that no adhesive wear was evident between the stainless-steel balls on the nickel-aluminum-bronze disc.

Abstract:
Coatings have historically been developed to provide protection against corrosion and erosion that is to protect the material from chemical and physical interaction with its environment. Corrosion and wear problems are still of great relevance in a wide range of industrial applications and products as they result in the degradation and eventual failure of components and systems both in the processing and manufacturing industries and in the service life of many components. Various technologies can be used to deposit the appropriate surface protection that can resist under specific conditions. They are usually distinguished by coating thickness: deposition of thin films (below 10 to 20 μm according to authors) and deposition of thick films. The latter, mostly produced at atmospheric pressure have a thickness over 30 μm, up to several millimeters and are used when the functional performance and life of component depend on the protective layer thickness. Both coating technology can also be divided into two distinct categories: "wet" and " dry " coating methods, the crucial difference being the medium in which the deposited material is processed. The former group mainly involves electroplating, electroless plating and hot-dip galvanizing while the second includes, among others methods, vapor deposition, thermal spray techniques, brazing, or weld overlays. This chapter deals with coatings deposited by thermal spraying. It is defined by Hermanek (2001) as follows , "Thermal spraying comprises a group of coating processes in which finely divided metallic or non-metallic materials are deposited in a molten or semi-molten condition to form a coating". The processes comprise: direct current (d.c.) arcs or radio frequency (r.f.) discharges-generated plasmas, plasma transferred arcs (PTA), wire arcs, flames, high velocity oxy-fuel flames (HVOF), high velocity air-fuel flames (HVAF), detonation guns (D-gun). Another spray technology has emerged recently ; it is called cold gas-dynamic spray technology, or Cold Spray (CS). It is not really a thermal spray technology as the high energy gas flow is produced by a compressed relatively cold gas (T < 800°C) expanding in a nozzle and will not be included in this presentation.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0921-5093(91)90870-s, doi:10.1016/0921-5093(91)90870-s. This article has 139 citations.

The excerpt identifies the NRL HPGA arrangement as a single chamber containing an induction-melting furnace, with the atomization nozzle mounted below the furnace. The spray is generated beneath the melting/atomization assembly and is then handled by downstream collection equipment. Powder collection is described as occurring through a centrifugal dust separator, followed by retention in a valved powder can (collection canister), as illustrated in Fig. 6. The available text does not provide the detailed geometry or operating function of a separately named spray chamber, nor does it explicitly explain a dedicated mechanism for protecting the collection system from liquid-metal splatter or un-atomized melt. It does, however, establish that the furnace and nozzle are housed in one chamber and that the powder is separated and retained downstream, rather than simply deposited directly in an open container. Any specific splatter-protection features—such as baffles, splash shields, melt traps, or chamber-wall deposition—would need to be obtained from Fig. 6 or another portion of the article, since they are not described in this excerpt.

The excerpt identifies the HPGA gas atomization system as having three principal sections: a melt chamber, a spray chamber, and a powder collection system. The melt chamber uses a high-purity alumina crucible and stopper rod, with a zirconia-coated pour tube guiding the molten Al-Si alloy through a 1.7 mm orifice to the HPGA nozzle. The nozzle has an annular arrangement of 30 gas jets around the melt feed tube. At the nozzle, the high-velocity gas creates a wake and local low-pressure region, while recirculating flow acts opposite to the melt-stream direction. These effects cause the stream to spread into a thin film, split, and accelerate outward, promoting atomization. However, this excerpt does not provide the detailed HPGA layout requested for a collection canister or cyclone separator, nor does it describe how collected powder is specifically protected from liquid-metal splatter or un-atomized melt. It only establishes that a separate powder collection system follows the spray chamber and that melt disintegration occurs near the nozzle and atomization zone.

Huimin Wang1,2    & Boian T. Alexandrov2 & Eric Przybylowicz2,3


Received: 17 December 2018 /Accepted: 22 February 2019 /Published online: 4 March 2019
# International Institute of Welding 2019

Abstract
Finite element analysis (FEA) model of the solidification process in the cast pin tear test (CPTT) was developed using the
commercial software ProCAST™. Modeling predictions of the solidification and strain accumulation sequences and of the
cracking sensitive region location were validated using parallel CPTT testing of Alloy 52M filler metal. Predicted pin length
dependences of the hot tearing indicator (HTI) and the effective plastic strain (EPS) were in good correlation with the experi-
mentally determined zero to 100% CPTT cracking curve in Alloy 52 M. Sensitivity study with the developed model identified
material properties and test parameters with strong influence on the accuracy of modeling predictions. Parallel computational
modeling and CPTT experimentation was performed to quantify the critical strain for solidification cracking in Alloy 52M filler
metal. This study demonstrated that numerical modeling of weldability tests can be used for quantification of material-specific
properties related to cracking susceptibility in engineering alloys.

Journal of Achievements in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering, 116:11-24, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393, doi:10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393. This article has 41 citations.

The excerpt describes a closed ultrasonic atomization system relevant to powder production, although it does not specifically identify the AMAZEMET system, aluminium bronze, a cooling cone, or detailed splatter-protection and container geometry. The atomization chamber contains the sonotrode, electric-arc melting zone, and cooled inert-gas flow. Molten-metal droplets are ejected into the cooled inert gas, where surface tension forms nearly spherical particles; the droplets then cool, solidify rapidly, and are carried toward the chamber outlet by aerodynamic forces. The warm gas and powder stream is sent to a cyclone separator. Powder is collected beneath the cyclone in a sealed container, while the gas is filtered to remove fine dust, cooled, and recirculated. The equipment is described as having separate raw-material delivery, melting, ultrasonic, cooling-gas/atomization-chamber, and gas-powder separation subsystems. The chamber operates under an inert-gas atmosphere, including during electric-arc ignition. The source indicates that integrated melting and atomization on the sonotrode helps avoid splashing associated with melting material above the sonotrode and draining it downward; earlier arrangements could produce interrupted atomization and poor-quality powder. However, no specific design details for a cooling cone, splash guard, container sealing mechanism, or AMAZEMET aluminium-bronze configuration are provided in this excerpt.

In arc-melting operation, metal vapor condenses on the chamber interior; this light, submicron deposit is removed by shaking, sonication, and rinsing before drying. These cleaning steps remove tiny high-surface-area particles and improve chemical properties. The excerpt therefore provides limited information relevant to collection and chamber cleanup, but no explicit engineering details about a cooling cone, collection container, or splash/splatter shielding.

### Artifact (ID artifact-03)

```python
# Adiabatic, lumped-capacitance screening calculation.
# C63000 is reported to have solidus/liquidus temperatures of about
# 1043/1060 °C; therefore, applying latent heat to all material at an
# assumed 1000 °C is deliberately conservative. (pqac-00000039)

m_bronze = 0.816       # kg [estimate]
T_bronze = 1000.0      # °C [estimate]
T_ambient = 25.0       # °C [estimate]

cp_bronze = 420.0      # J/(kg·K), Cu-Al-Ni bronze estimate
latent_bronze = 205000 # J/kg, conservative Cu-alloy estimate
cp_ss316l = 500.0      # J/(kg·K), temperature-averaged estimate
cp_copper = 385.0      # J/(kg·K), temperature-averaged estimate

scenarios = {
    "1 kg 316L only":             {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 0.0},
    "1 kg 316L + 0.5 kg Cu":      {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 0.5},
    "1 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu":        {"ss316l": 1.0, "copper": 1.0},
    "3 kg 316L only":             {"ss316l": 3.0, "copper": 0.0},
    "3 kg 316L + 1 kg Cu":        {"ss316l": 3.0, "copper": 1.0},
}


def equilibrium_temperature(m_ss, m_cu, include_latent):
    """Return adiabatic equilibrium temperature in °C."""
    receiver_heat_capacity = m_ss * cp_ss316l + m_cu * cp_copper
    numerator = (
        m_bronze * cp_bronze * T_bronze
        + receiver_heat_capacity * T_ambient
    )
    if include_latent:
        numerator += m_bronze * latent_bronze

    denominator = m_bronze * cp_bronze + receiver_heat_capacity
    return numerator / denominator


print(f"{'Configuration':<30} {'Full latent heat':>18} {'No latent heat':>18}")
print("-" * 70)

for name, masses in scenarios.items():
    with_latent = equilibrium_temperature(
        masses["ss316l"], masses["copper"], include_latent=True
    )
    without_latent = equilibrium_temperature(
        masses["ss316l"], masses["copper"], include_latent=False
    )
    print(f"{name:<30} {with_latent:>15.1f} °C {without_latent:>15.1f} °C")

# Expected approximate output:
# 1 kg 316L only                    620.0 °C           421.0 °C
# 1 kg 316L + 0.5 kg Cu             508.8 °C           347.7 °C
